summary: Teach the shared language of geometric diagram markings as statements of relationships, not pictures: a small square asserts exactly 90°, a matching pair of single tick marks asserts 'these two lengths are equal to each other', a second independent equal pair uses double ticks, matching arc marks assert equal angles, and arrows assert parallel lines. Three-letter notation ∠ABC names the angle whose vertex is the MIDDLE letter (B), with arms BA and BC. Fluency runs in two directions — reading a marked diagram to extract the given facts, and adding correct marks when drawing. Critically, a geometric diagram carries stated facts and is not a scale drawing: the marks override the picture's appearance.
misconceptions: Reads ∠ABC as the angle at the first (or last) letter rather than the middle letter (the vertex)
Reads tick marks as a measurement or length value rather than 'equal to each other', or treats single and double ticks as equal to one another
Treats the marks as decoration and judges lengths, angles and right angles from the diagram's appearance (assumes it is drawn to scale)
Thinks the small square is just 'a corner' rather than exactly 90°, or misses that unmarked features are unknown

activities.title: Mark up a plain figure, then read a 'not to scale' one
steps: Starting from a plain quadrilateral (a four-sided figure gives room to show two independent equal-side pairs without overlap), add a small square to the corner stated to be right-angled.

Add a single pair of tick marks to one pair of sides stated to be equal, and a double pair of ticks to a different, independent pair of equal sides — a four-sided figure is needed so the two pairs do not share a side.
Label a stated angle in three-letter notation by identifying its vertex: point to the vertex B first, then trace the two arms BA and BC, so the middle letter B names the angle ∠ABC.
Switch to reading: on a deliberately not-to-scale marked diagram where one side LOOKS longer but carries the matching tick, state which sides are equal from the marks, not the picture.
State aloud what each mark means as a relationship (e.g. 'these two sides are equal to each other', 'this angle is exactly 90°').
activities.insight: The marks, not the drawing, tell you the truth about a diagram, and the middle letter of three-letter notation is always the vertex.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal the mark key (reading scaffold)
steps: Tap the small square to reveal 'this angle is exactly 90°'.
Tap a tick pair and see the two equal sides highlight together.
Tap ∠ABC and see the vertex B with its arms BA and BC light up.
Say each meaning aloud before revealing it, then check against the reveal.
activities.insight: Each symbol in the mark key encodes a specific relationship that can be read off a diagram reliably.

activities.title: Match and select: check interpretation and light production
steps: Answer 'Which angle is ∠ABC?' by selecting the angle at vertex B, not the angle at A or C.
Match each mark (square, single tick pair, double tick pair, arc pair, arrows) to its meaning.
Mark the equal sides on a figure by selecting/drawing the pair that carries matching ticks.
On a not-to-scale item, identify equal sides from the marks even when one side looks longer.
activities.insight: Both interpreting marks and identifying where marks belong can be checked explicitly, including the middle-letter vertex rule.

activities.title: Probe diagram authority and unmarked features
steps: Answer: 'This side LOOKS longer than that one, but both carry a single tick — which is actually longer?' (Answer: they are equal.)
Show ∠BCA on the same diagram and decide whether it is the same as ∠ABC or a different angle.
Decide what mark to add for a second pair of equal sides so no one confuses it with the first pair (double ticks).
Answer: 'This corner has no square drawn on it — can you be sure it's a right angle? How would the diagram tell you?' (You cannot assume it; unmarked features are unknown.)
activities.insight: Marks are authoritative, three-letter names with different middle letters (vertices) denote different angles (though reversing the outer letters, as in ∠ABC and ∠CBA, names the same angle), and an unmarked feature is not a stated fact.

checkQuestion: Show a triangle marked with a small square at one corner, single tick marks on two of its sides, and one angle named ∠ABC. First (read): 'What does the small square tell you? What do the tick marks tell you? Which angle is ∠ABC — point to it.' Then (produce): 'On this second plain diagram, mark a right angle with the correct symbol, and show that two of its sides are equal in length.'
checkAnswer: Reads the small square as 'this angle is exactly 90°', the tick marks as 'these two sides are equal in length', and identifies ∠ABC as the angle at vertex B (the middle letter); and on the plain diagram draws a small square in a corner to denote 90° and adds a matching pair of tick marks to two sides to denote equal lengths.
